title: Thermal Hall Signatures of Distinct Schwinger-Boson Flux Sectors on the Honeycomb Lattice
abstract: Thermal transport offers a bulk probe of charge-neutral excitations in frustrated magnets. It remains challenging, however, to determine whether such transport can distinguish different parton mean-field structures of the same spin system. This question is particularly relevant on the honeycomb lattice, where distinct $0$-flux, $π$-flux, and chiral $π/2$-flux sectors have been proposed. In this paper, we compare self-consistent saddle-point solutions in these three sectors for a frustrated $J_1-J_2$ Heisenberg model with a next-nearest-neighbor Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction and a perpendicular magnetic field. Using finite-temperature Schwinger-boson mean-field theory and the Kubo formula for bosonic Bogoliubov-de Gennes systems, we evaluate the intrinsic spinon thermal Hall conductivity. At a common parameter point where all three branches remain gapped, the $0$-flux response is positive and the $π$-flux response is negative for $D>0$ and $h>0$ under the sign conventions used in this paper, whereas the $π/2$-flux response changes sign with increasing temperature. We further show that a projective symmetry combining a sixfold rotation with time reversal forces the zero-field response of a fixed chiral $π/2$-flux domain to vanish. Within the mean-field regime examined in this paper, the sign and temperature dependence of $κ_{xy}/T$ therefore provide a flux-sensitive transport signature.
summary: This theoretical work investigates how thermal transport can distinguish between different mean-field descriptions (flux sectors) of a frustrated Heisenberg magnet on the honeycomb lattice. By calculating the spinon thermal Hall conductivity using Schwinger-boson mean-field theory, the authors demonstrate that the sign and temperature dependence of this conductivity serve as a unique, flux-sensitive signature.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of using thermal transport to distinguish between different mean-field structures (flux sectors) within a single frustrated quantum spin system.
main_result: The sign and temperature dependence of the intrinsic spinon thermal Hall conductivity ($\kappa_{xy}/T$) provide a flux-sensitive transport signature, with distinct behaviors observed for 0-flux, $\pi$-flux, and $\pi/2$-flux sectors.
method: The analysis employs Schwinger-boson mean-field theory combined with the Kubo formula for bosonic Bogoliubov-de Gennes systems to calculate the thermal Hall conductivity.
model_or_system: The system is a spin-1/2 Heisenberg model on the honeycomb lattice, extended with a next-nearest-neighbor Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction and a perpendicular magnetic field.
key_observables: Intrinsic spinon thermal Hall conductivity ($\kappa_{xy}$), the energy-resolved thermal kernel $I_T(\epsilon)$, and the connected dynamical structure factor $S(\mathbf{q}, \omega)$.
important_parameters: The analysis compares three flux sectors: 0-flux, $\pi$-flux, and chiral $\pi/2$-flux, across varying magnetic field ($h$) and DM interaction ($D$) strengths.
main_assumptions: The calculations rely on the Schwinger-boson mean-field approximation and specific decoupling approximations for the bond operators.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the lattice structure and the three distinct mean-field Ansätze (0-, $\pi$-, $\pi/2$-flux). Supporting figures show the energy-resolved origin of the $\pi/2$-flux sign reversal and the connected dynamical structure factor $S(\mathbf{q}, \omega)$ for the different flux sectors.
paper_structure: The paper systematically develops the mean-field Hamiltonian for the three flux sectors, calculates the thermal Hall conductivity using the Kubo formula, and analyzes the resulting spectral features and temperature dependencies to establish the flux-sensitive diagnostic.
why_interesting: The use of thermal transport as a diagnostic tool to probe subtle, non-local quantum order (flux sectors) in frustrated magnets is highly relevant to understanding exotic phases in strongly correlated materials.
